name: Hair dryer giant stationary (1930s)

card.summary: Large salon hair dryers of the early twentieth century, fixed or pedestal machines used to dry and set hair for waves and styles.
card.aka: Salon pedestal dryer; early bonnet dryer
card.note: Early electric dryers carried overheating and shock risks.

quick.overview:
Before compact handheld dryers, hair was dried by large stationary machines in salons. The first, built by French stylist Alexandre Godefroy in 1888, was a bonnet connected to the chimney of a gas stove.

By the 1930s, pedestal and wall-type dryers in salons dried hair quickly enough to hold waves and sets, making styled hair possible in the salon chair.
quick.how: A client sat beneath a hood or bonnet while warm air dried and set the hair, often after permanent waving or curling. Operators ran them in the salon rather than at home.
quick.risks: Early electrical dryers had overheating and electrocution risks; safety rules such as the 1991 US ground-fault requirement came later.

lead: Giant stationary hair dryers were the large salon machines used before lightweight handheld models took over. The first hair dryer is credited to French stylist Alexandre Godefroy, who in 1888 made a large stationary bonnet attached to a gas stove chimney for his salon.[1]

In the 1920s and 1930s salon equipment grew more elaborate, with pedestal dryers and permanent-wave apparatus; one manufacturer, Icall, used Bakelite for hand-held dryer casings and pedestal dryer linings because it resisted corrosion and reduced the risk of burning the stylist's fingers.[2] Later the bonnet dryer reached consumers in 1951 and the rigid-hood dryer appeared in the 1950s.[1]

chain: Client sits under large hood or bonnet
Warm air dries wet or waved hair quickly
Set waves and curls hold their shape
angle.text: The machines dried hair evenly and fast enough to set waves and curls in the salon. They made polished, styled hair a routine salon service.

paras: Godefroy's 1888 invention was a large stationary bonnet.[1] A US patent followed in 1911 to Gabriel Kazanjian.[1] Handheld models reached the market around 1920 but were heavy, about 1 kg, and drew roughly 100 W, with overheating and electrocution risks.[1] Stationary salon machines remained the standard way to dry set hair.[1]
Permanent-wave machines of the period used a wheeled vertical pipe carrying a "chandelier" holding up to 22 heaters, and Bakelite casings appeared in dryers and heater parts.[2]

US safety guidelines for dryers came in the 1970s and in 1991 the Consumer Product Safety Commission required ground fault circuit interrupters; reported dryer-related deaths fell below two per year by 2000.[1]

timeline.event: Godefroy builds the first hair dryer.[1]
